name: Pink Oyster: bright pink
summary: Warm and blue-lit from pinning on, then picked young, for strong pink color and a fuller harvest than a dim grow.
notes: Pick young, as soon as the caps open and before the edges turn up.
chamber_notes: Do not cold-shock. Chamber limits: there is no heater or cooler, so temperature targets only hold if the room sits near them. There is no CO2 sensor, so the fan schedule stands in for fresh air. The humidifier can only add moisture, so a low humidity target depends on dry room air.

source_notes.title: Guzman-de-Casa et al. 2026, blue light in five mushrooms
source_notes.detail: Plant Foods for Human Nutrition (2026). Blue light at 8 h a day raised P. djamor biological efficiency by 428% compared with darkness and gave normal pigmented fruits. Darkness gave long stipes, weak color, and malformed fruits. The comparison was blue light against darkness, not against white light.

source_notes.title: Chowdhury et al. 2024, pink oyster
source_notes.detail: BioResources 19(1), 2024. P. djamor grows well up to 30 °C, with mycelium best at 24 to 28 °C, and fruits within 1 to 2 weeks of conditions being right.

source_notes.title: Stamets
source_notes.detail: Paul Stamets, Growing Gourmet and Medicinal Mushrooms (commonly cited chamber ranges). P. djamor is a warm-weather species, often fruited 20 to 30 °C.

stages.name: Blue fruiting
stages.notes: Color fades as fruits mature; harvest while still vivid.

light_recipe.why: Blue only at 8 h a day, the schedule that gave pigmented fruits and a large yield gain over darkness in the 2026 study.
light_recipe.wavelength_note: WS2812 red is roughly 620 to 630 nm and blue roughly 465 to 475 nm. The RGB mix is an approximation of the cited wavelengths, not a measured spectrum. RGB percent is LED drive level, not a photon ratio.
